stories.bridge: Before you study the Hermetic foundations as a system, sit with how they arrived — carried a thousand years, translated in a hurry on a banker's orders, powerful enough to bend the Renaissance. Now let's open the Corpus itself.

figures.name: Hermes Trismegistus
figures.role: Legendary attributed author of the Hermetic texts

figures.name: Marsilio Ficino
figures.role: Florentine scholar; translated the Corpus into Latin

figures.name: Isaac Casaubon
figures.role: Classical scholar; dated the Corpus to the post-Christian era

stories.hook: In 1463, Cosimo de' Medici ordered his young scholar Marsilio Ficino to stop translating Plato. A Greek manuscript had just arrived in Florence, and it could not wait.
stories.narrative: The manuscript was a collection of dialogues attributed to Hermes Trismegistus — 'Hermes the Thrice-Greatest' — a figure who fused the Greek god Hermes with the Egyptian god Thoth. The texts themselves had been written in Greek in Roman Egypt, in the second and third centuries of the common era, by anonymous philosophers who believed they were recording primeval wisdom. For over a thousand years they circulated in fragments, half-forgotten. Then, in 1460, a monk carried a complete Greek copy to Florence, and Cosimo de' Medici — the banker who effectively ruled the city — decided this took precedence over everything, even Plato. Ficino set Plato aside and translated the Corpus Hermeticum into Latin, finishing in 1463. It was printed in 1471, and Renaissance Europe caught fire. Pico della Mirandola wove it into his defense of human dignity. Giordano Bruno preached it across Europe. John Dee — the English mathematician you will meet in this course — treated Hermes as an authority second only to scripture. The most famous line attributed to the tradition, 'as above, so below,' comes from the Emerald Tablet, a short companion text. Here is the honest twist, and it matters for how you read esoteric texts: in 1614, the scholar Isaac Casaubon used linguistic analysis to show the Corpus could not be as ancient as claimed — its Greek betrayed a post-Christian date. The debunking was devastating and correct. And yet the texts' influence did not die, because their power was never really about their age. They had given the Renaissance a vocabulary for the idea that the human mind participates in the cosmos — an idea that fed both modern science and modern magic. The word 'hermetic' itself survives in your kitchen: a hermetically sealed jar is sealed, as the old texts said, with the secret art of Hermes.
stories.title: The story behind the Corpus Hermeticum
verifiedClaims: Ficino completed his Latin translation of the Corpus Hermeticum in 1463 at Cosimo de' Medici's direction
The translation was first printed in 1471
Isaac Casaubon demonstrated in 1614 that the texts date from the post-Christian era, not remote antiquity
The surviving Greek texts were composed in Roman Egypt in the 2nd–3rd centuries CE

stories.bridge: You are about to study a system dictated letter by letter over seven years and recorded like experimental data. Keep Dee's double identity in mind — the rigorous mathematician and the angel-caller were the same person. Let's enter the sessions.

figures.name: John Dee
figures.role: Mathematician, astronomer, advisor to Elizabeth I

figures.name: Edward Kelley
figures.role: Scryer; Dee's partner in the angelic workings

stories.hook: In the spring of 1582, in a house in Mortlake outside London, the queen's astrologer began taking dictation from angels.
stories.narrative: John Dee was the most learned Englishman of his age: mathematician, astronomer, navigator — the man who taught England's sailors to cross oceans, who coined the phrase 'British Empire,' and who advised Queen Elizabeth I herself on matters ranging from calendar reform to the succession. He was also convinced that mathematics and angelic communication were part of the same science, and that the Book of Nature had a second volume most scholars never opened. In 1582 he met Edward Kelley, a young man with a talent for scrying — gazing into a crystal or a black mirror and reporting visions. Together they began a series of 'actions,' or sessions, that would continue for seven years, across England, Poland, and the court of Emperor Rudolf II in Prague, where the emperor's famous tolerance for occultists gave them shelter. The method never varied: Kelley would stare into the stone and describe what he saw — angels, tablets, letters appearing in grids — while Dee, meticulous as any laboratory scientist, wrote down everything. The result is thousands of pages of diaries, still preserved, recording the sessions almost like experimental data. What came through, they believed, was a language: Enochian, named for the biblical Enoch, who 'walked with God.' It had its own alphabet, grammar, and vocabulary, delivered letter by letter, sometimes backwards, sometimes in elaborate tables. The crown of the system was the 48 Calls, or Keys — long invocations in the angelic tongue, each opening, they said, a different region of creation. Dee never published the material; after his death in 1609 the manuscripts slept for centuries, until the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn revived them in the 1890s and Aleister Crowley carried them into the twentieth century. Modern linguists who have studied Enochian note something curious: whatever its source, it behaves like a real language, with consistent internal structure — which is why the debate about it has never ended. Dee himself embodied the bridge this course walks: the same man who wrote the Monas Hieroglyphica, a work of mathematical mysticism published in 1564, spent his evenings asking angels for the keys to creation. He saw no contradiction. Neither, for the purposes of this module, should you — study the system on its own terms first, and judge the metaphysics later. A final detail worth carrying into the module: Dee's diaries show the sessions were collaborative and contested — Kelley sometimes refused to scry, Dee sometimes doubted what came through, and the "angels" themselves set conditions. Whatever you believe crossed the crystal, the record shows two men negotiating with the unknown for seven years, in three countries, with a queen's favor on the line.
stories.title: The story behind Enochian
verifiedClaims: Dee and Kelley's angelic workings ran from 1582 to 1589
Dee was advisor to Queen Elizabeth I and author of Monas Hieroglyphica (1564)
The workings produced the Enochian language and the 48 Calls/Keys, recorded in Dee's diaries
The Golden Dawn revived Enochian material in the 1890s

stories.bridge: You are about to enter the CCRU seminar, where cybernetics escapes the laboratory and starts rewriting reality. Remember Wiener's steersman — because hyperstition is what happens when the feedback loop closes around belief itself.

figures.name: Gregory Bateson
figures.role: Anthropologist; carried cybernetics into the social sciences

stories.hook: In 1948, an MIT mathematician named a new science after the Greek word for 'steersman' — and claimed it governed machines, animals, and societies alike.
stories.narrative: Norbert Wiener was a child prodigy — a PhD from Harvard at eighteen — who had spent the Second World War on an unglamorous problem: predicting where an enemy airplane would be by the time an anti-aircraft shell arrived. Working with the engineer Julian Bigelow, he discovered that the mathematics of aiming a gun — measure, predict, correct, repeat — was the mathematics of feedback, and that feedback appeared everywhere: in thermostats, in nervous systems, in economies. In 1948 he published 'Cybernetics: or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine,' naming the field from the Greek kybernetes, steersman — the same root as 'governor.' The book argued something radical: that control and communication were one subject, whether the system was built of copper or of cells. From 1946 to 1953, the Macy Conferences in New York brought together an astonishing roster — the neurophysiologist Warren McCulloch, John von Neumann, the anthropologists Gregory Bateson and Margaret Mead — to hammer out what this meant. Out of those rooms came systems theory, early AI, family therapy, and the conceptual vocabulary of feedback loops that still runs through engineering. Wiener himself grew uneasy with his creation; late in life he warned that automated systems would make decisions whose consequences no one had chosen, and he refused military funding on principle. Half a century later, at the University of Warwick, a small philosophy collective called the CCRU — the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit, founded in 1995 by Sadie Plant and soon driven by Nick Land — picked up Wiener's thread and pulled it somewhere stranger. Where Wiener studied how systems steer themselves, the CCRU asked what happens when ideas steer systems: their concept of hyperstition — fictions that make themselves real through feedback — is cybernetics turned on culture itself. A rumor about a currency moves markets; the market movement confirms the rumor. The steersman now steers the stories that steer the steersman. That loop — which Wiener mapped in machines and the CCRU mapped in myth — is the engine room of this seminar. Wiener would have recognized the pattern instantly: a signal leaves the system, the environment reacts, the reaction returns as input. The CCRU simply noticed that the signal could be a story and the environment could be a market, a subculture, a timeline. Cybernetics began by steering anti-aircraft guns; it ends, for our purposes, by asking who steers the steersman when the feedback loop is made of belief.
stories.title: The story behind cybernetics
verifiedClaims: His wartime work concerned anti-aircraft fire prediction with Julian Bigelow
